items.title: 12.2.3 Synthesis of ammonia from ammonium salts

source_refs.note: Topic 12.2.3 with Figure 12.3 and Quick Check 12.1, printed page 275.

blocks.text: In the laboratory, ammonia gas can be synthesized by heating an ammonium salt such as ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) with a base like calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂) as shown in Figure 12.3.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: There is no sodium in the reactants, so NaCl cannot form; calcium chloride forms. The printed equation is also not balanced. The balanced equation is 2NH₄Cl(s) + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O(l) + 2NH₃(g).

In this acid-base reaction, NH₄⁺ acts as an acid by donating H⁺ ions, while OH⁻ acts as a base by accepting H⁺ ions. This reaction displaces ammonia gas from the ammonium salt and produces salt and water. It is commonly used to identify ammonium in salt analysis. If a gas with a pungent smell is released and turns moistened red litmus paper blue, it indicates the presence of ammonium in the compound.

blocks.alt: Laboratory set-up. A boiling tube holding a white solid mixture is clamped to a stand and heated at its closed end by a burner; its mouth slopes slightly down and is closed by a cork. A delivery tube runs to the foot of a drying tower packed with white lumps. A tube from the top of the tower enters an inverted gas jar held by a second stand; arrows at the mouth of the jar show air escaping. Pointer arrows mark the mixture, the lumps and the jar.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.3: Synthesis of ammonia gas (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 12.3 clamps the test tube with the heated closed end low and the mouth raised. The tube should slope slightly downwards towards its mouth, as drawn above, so that the water formed does not run back onto the hot glass and crack it.
